analysis.one_liner: Extends credit discrimination protections and adds criminal penalties for discriminatory lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with three cosponsors, never received a House committee markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the Equal Credit Opportunity Act to bar lenders from discriminating based on sexual orientation, gender identity, or where an applicant lives (zip code or census tract). It would have created a new office inside the consumer protection bureau that uses undercover testers to catch discriminatory lending, required reviews of loan applications for illegal bias, added criminal penalties — including personal fines and prison time for executives who direct a pattern of discrimination — and expanded mortgage-lending data collection.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who belong to protected classes, especially LGBTQ applicants, people living in low-income or majority-minority neighborhoods who are denied credit because of where they live, and anyone wrongly denied credit. The bill would also give the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Justice Department stronger tools to catch and punish discrimination.

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, so lenders could not lawfully reject or price a loan because of them.
Bars discrimination based on an applicant's zip code or census tract, targeting the practice of denying or worse-pricing credit based on neighborhood rather than the applicant's own qualifications.

Creates an Office of Fair Lending Testing inside the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau that sends undercover 'testers' posing as borrowers to lenders, and refers suspected violations to the Attorney General.

Adds criminal penalties: up to a $50,000 fine or one year in prison for a knowing violation, up to $100,000 per violation and 20 years' imprisonment for a pattern of discrimination, and for executives who direct such a pattern, a fine of up to 100% of their compensation and up to five years in prison.
Requires the consumer bureau to review lenders' loan applications and processes and prohibit and penalize any that violate the Equal Credit Opportunity Act or other federal consumer financial law.

Expands Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data collection to include sexual orientation and other applicant characteristics, giving regulators and researchers more complete evidence of lending disparities.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, mortgage lenders, and other creditors would face new compliance costs, undercover testing of their lending practices, expanded data reporting, and for the first time criminal exposure — including personal fines and prison terms for executives — for discriminatory lending. Taxpayers would fund the new testing office.

drawbacks.text: Criminal penalties for lending discrimination could capture conduct that is statistically complex to prove; lending decisions involve thousands of factors, and the threat of prison for underwriting staff and executives could make some lenders more conservative about extending credit to applicants in lower-income or riskier neighborhoods, the very groups the bill aims to help.

Restricting the use of zip code and census tract in credit decisions while simultaneously requiring lenders to report that same data could raise compliance disputes, and a tester-based enforcement system adds a new federal bureaucracy with ongoing taxpayer cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits for borrowers facing discrimination are real and specific, and its enforcement tools (testers, criminal exposure for executives) are considerably stronger than existing civil-only penalties. The costs are real too: compliance burden on lenders, some risk of over-deterrence in credit access, and the price of a new federal office. On balance it is a strong pro-borrower measure with an aggressive enforcement design whose workability would depend on how criminal provisions were applied.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee never took the bill up, and it never reached the House floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Al Green introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced.
It drew three cosponsors, all House Democrats, and received no further action for the remainder of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Creditors and lenders benefited: with the bill dead, discriminatory-lending practices remained subject only to existing civil enforcement, and executives faced no new criminal or personal liability. Borrowers in protected classes, including LGBTQ applicants and residents of neighborhoods targeted by lenders, got no new protection.

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Lending for All Act on January 3, 2019.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill out during the two-year Congress, leaving it without any vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and no House Republican support is recorded; the bill never advanced far enough for a floor vote to reveal a fuller partisan split.

industries.industry: Banks, mortgage lenders, and consumer credit companies
industries.note: The bill would have imposed new protected classes, undercover compliance testing, expanded data reporting, and criminal penalties including executive-level fines and prison time for discriminatory lending. Its defeat left lenders under existing civil-only fair-lending enforcement.
The bill would have created a new fair-lending testing office and expanded the bureau's authority to review and prohibit discriminatory loan applications. Its budget would grow accordingly.
